Independent-minded and uncomfortable with following a crowd merely because something is popular.
Cautious in unfamiliar settings, but not so fearful that they avoid all novelty.
Sensitive to criticism and prone to replaying a sharp comment later, even when they appear calm.
Dryly funny with trusted people, especially about minor inconveniences and family logistics.
Generally cooperative, but increasingly firm when their boundaries or identity are dismissed.
Hopeful in short bursts rather than relentlessly optimistic; a concrete plan can restore their energy.
Sometimes procrastinates on schoolwork when home responsibilities and paid work pile up.
Likes being useful and competent, but has to remind themselves they are allowed to ask for help.
Values privacy and dislikes being pressured to share personal feelings in a group.

openness.description: High. Kiran is interested in unfamiliar cultures, art, history, food, languages, and ways of organizing daily life. They enjoy learning but prefer substance over novelty for its own sake.

conscientiousness.description: Moderate to moderately high. They are responsible about work shifts, travel costs, and family commitments, though school organization can slip when they are tired or overcommitted.

extraversion.description: Low to moderate. They prefer a small group, need quiet time after busy days, and can participate comfortably when there is a shared activity or clear purpose.

agreeableness.description: Moderately high. They are considerate and patient, but not endlessly accommodating; they can be skeptical or blunt if someone is being unfair or dismissive.

neuroticism.description: Moderately elevated. Uncertainty, money stress, and social judgment can produce rumination or physical nervousness. Reassurance helps most when it comes with accurate information and a practical next step.

interests: Urban transit systems, especially subway maps and how different cities connect neighborhoods.
Street photography and taking pictures of signs, storefronts, window displays, and changing light.
Art museums, especially exhibits that explain who made the work and the context around it.
History told through everyday objects, food, buildings, and family stories.
Environmental issues when discussed through specific local effects rather than abstract slogans.
Playlists shared by friends and music that works well on a long train ride.
Trying new foods when there is a familiar option available if they do not like it.
Public libraries, used bookstores, and places where they can browse without being hurried.
travel_preferences: The Europe trip is a family trip, not a solo trip or a trip with a romantic partner; Kiran expects to travel with their mother, maternal grandmother, and younger brother.
The family is looking at a summer 2027 trip, but dates depend on work schedules, school, and how much they can save.
They are most interested in London, with Paris as a possible second stop only if the extra transport and lodging do not make the trip too rushed or expensive.
They would rather spend several nights in one place than change hotels every day.
They want a package that makes flights and lodging easy to compare, but do not assume a package is automatically cheaper.
They want a clear, itemized total price with taxes, baggage, transfers, and cancellation rules explained before anyone pays.
Their family's aspirational all-in budget is limited; a quote that looks affordable before meals and local transit can still be out of reach.
They prefer economy flights with reasonable layovers over a luxury cabin or an exhausting itinerary designed to save a small amount.
They are willing to take a train between European cities if the price, luggage arrangements, and station connections are straightforward.
They want some planned activities but do not want a guided tour to occupy every hour.
One major museum or landmark in a day feels manageable; stacking several timed attractions feels like homework.
They like leaving open time for a neighborhood walk, a market, or an unplanned café stop.
They would check recent reviews from several sources rather than trust a single influencer or polished package description.
They pay attention to whether a hotel is close to a usable transit stop, not simply whether it is described as central.
They want a private family room or adjoining rooms rather than a shared dormitory.
A private bathroom matters, particularly because the family has different routines and their grandmother values privacy.
A working elevator is important because their grandmother has some knee stiffness and does not want to climb several flights with luggage.
They prefer clean, plain, well-maintained lodging over ornate décor or a prestigious hotel name.
A basic breakfast included in the room rate is attractive if the price is genuinely reasonable.
Reliable air conditioning matters during hot weather, but they will check whether it is actually available rather than assume it.
They would appreciate a small fridge, a safe place for documents, and a front desk that is staffed at night.
They are moderately safety-conscious: they want secure doors, a well-lit route back, and sensible arrival instructions, but do not want travel marketed through fear.
They prefer to know how late public transit runs and what the backup plan is if the family misses the last train.
They want staff to use their chosen name and pronouns where practical, while understanding that airline and passport records must match legal documents.
They would feel more comfortable with a hotel that has clear policies and respectful staff than with one selling itself as trendy or exclusive.
They are wary of prepaid, nonrefundable bookings because the household cannot easily absorb a sudden change or lost payment.
They want the family to have a modest emergency reserve rather than spend every available dollar on attractions.
They would rather buy lunch from a bakery, market, or casual neighborhood restaurant than pay for expensive hotel dining every day.
They like one or two familiar food options nearby, especially for their younger brother and grandmother.
They will use reviews and friends' recommendations as a reality check, but do not want to visit a place solely because it is viral.
They hope to use trains, buses, and walking where practical, while recognizing that their family may need taxis occasionally for fatigue or luggage.
They want travel insurance explained in plain language, including exclusions and how a claim would actually be made.
They are not seeking luxury extras such as a spa, concierge, minibar, or private tour; they would rather spend money on a comfortable room and a memorable activity.
They like having a basic itinerary saved offline, along with addresses and booking confirmations, in case mobile service fails.
general_likes: A seat by the subway window when the train is not crowded.
Independent shops where browsing does not create pressure to buy.
A good neighborhood bakery and a warm pastry after a long shift.
Quiet museum galleries where people can look without being pushed along.
Maps that show street names clearly and do not hide practical details behind illustrations.
Taking photographs for themselves rather than posting every outing.
Playlists with a mix of familiar songs and a few discoveries.
A shared meal where everyone can choose something within their budget.
Clear explanations from adults who do not talk down to them.
Having enough time to change their mind before making a purchase.
Libraries with comfortable corners and staff who give useful recommendations.
Weather that is cool enough to walk in without getting sweaty.
Small souvenirs with a story, such as a postcard or transit ticket, rather than expensive branded goods.
A family plan that includes breaks and does not assume the youngest person has unlimited energy.
Seeing an ordinary residential street as well as the famous landmarks.
dislikes: Surprise charges that appear only at checkout.
Sales language that describes a trip as a once-in-a-lifetime deal and pressures people to book immediately.
Hotels with beautiful lobby photographs but vague information about room size, elevators, or location.
People assuming a teenager cannot understand a budget or itinerary.
Adults using their pronouns correctly only when reminded in public, then forgetting in private.
Crowded attractions where the experience becomes mostly waiting in a queue.
A schedule with early starts every day and no recovery time.
Being told to stop worrying without anyone answering the question they asked.
Food waste, disposable plastic used by default, and green claims that are not backed by specifics.
Online reviews that seem copied, exaggerated, or written to punish staff for one minor inconvenience.
Having to choose between helping at home and keeping up with school.
Expensive souvenirs that look mass-produced but are presented as locally meaningful.
Being photographed without permission, especially in a way that makes their gender presentation a spectacle.
Plans that assume every family member wants the same pace, food, or activities.

beliefs: A person should be able to ask how much something costs without being made to feel cheap.
A low advertised price is not a good deal if important fees are hidden until later.
Travel is valuable partly because it helps make other people's lives feel less abstract.
A trip does not have to be luxurious to be meaningful.
A comfortable, clean, well-located room matters more to them than a famous hotel brand.
A safe trip depends on preparation and respect, not on treating every unfamiliar place as dangerous.
It is sensible to check local conditions and transport options without letting worst-case stories run the whole itinerary.
People should be allowed to make different choices about gender expression without having to prove that those choices are permanent.
Using someone's name and pronouns is a basic sign of respect, not a special favor.
They can be patient with honest mistakes, but repeated dismissiveness is different from an honest mistake.
Being sixteen does not mean their observations about money, comfort, or logistics are automatically wrong.
Adults should make final legal and financial decisions for a minor while still listening seriously to that minor's preferences.
Family responsibility matters, but children should not have to become substitute adults for the whole household.
A reliable public transit system gives people more freedom, especially when they cannot afford a car or frequent taxis.
Walking and trains are good ways to understand a city, provided the route and the group's needs make that practical.
Environmental protection matters even when people have limited choices and cannot afford the most expensive low-impact option.
A person should not be shamed for taking an airplane when family distance, price, or time makes other options unrealistic.
Companies should be specific about what makes a tourism offer environmentally responsible instead of relying on vague labels.
Popular places can be worth visiting, but popularity alone does not make an experience right for their family.
Recommendations from trusted friends are useful, but the family should still compare the facts for themselves.
Online reviews can reveal patterns, but one angry or glowing review is not enough to establish what a hotel is like.
A good itinerary leaves room for rest, mistakes, and spontaneous discoveries.
A family holiday should not become a test of who can endure the most packed schedule.
Local businesses deserve consideration, but they do not need to be romanticized or treated as automatically better than chains.
Tourism should not make residents' daily lives harder just so visitors can get a photograph.
Museums and historic sites are more meaningful when they explain difficult history honestly, not only celebrate famous people.
It is okay to enjoy a place without understanding every detail of its history, as long as visitors remain curious and respectful.
Religious traditions can matter deeply to family members even when Kiran does not share their faith.
Kiran is secular and agnostic; they do not need religious belief to care about kindness, responsibility, or community.
Family stories can hold several versions of the same event, and the disagreement does not always mean one person is lying.
Knowing fragments of a heritage language is still a connection, though it is not the same as fluency.
People should not be expected to represent an entire culture because of their name or family background.
Money stress is a circumstance, not proof that a family is irresponsible or undeserving of enjoyable experiences.
It is better to save for an emergency than to spend every last dollar trying to make a trip look impressive.
A plan that can be changed without a large penalty is worth paying somewhat more for when a family's circumstances are unstable.
When information is confusing, asking a trusted adult or customer-service representative to explain it is responsible, not embarrassing.
They are interested in climate action but do not identify with a settled political party or enjoy arguments that turn every issue into team loyalty.
skills: Uses New York City buses and subways confidently and can compare routes, transfers, and walking distances.
Can read transit maps and identify when a route looks simple on paper but involves a difficult transfer.
Searches several sources for hotel and package information and notices when terms or totals do not match.
Keeps screenshots of important details and can organize links and notes in a shared phone document.
Has practical cash-handling skills from work and knows when to ask a supervisor rather than guess.
Speaks English fluently, conversational Spanish, and familiar Sinhala greetings and household expressions.
Takes thoughtful phone photographs and has a good eye for signs, framing, and changes in light.
Can prepare a few simple meals and snacks for themself and their younger brother.
Can help their grandmother navigate basic smartphone settings, video calls, and text messages.
Notices when a friend or family member is getting overwhelmed, though they are still learning not to take responsibility for fixing every mood.
Can compare the practical value of a hotel amenity against its actual price.
Is comfortable asking specific questions when given a little time to prepare, but finds surprise phone calls harder than written communication.

general: Checks the total price twice and sometimes takes a screenshot so they can show their mother the exact wording later.
Keeps transit cards, school identification, and work papers in separate pockets to avoid losing them in a rushed morning.
Tends to observe a group for a while before joining a conversation.
When uncertain, sends a short text to their mother rather than making a financial commitment on the spot.
Uses a notes app to collect travel links, possible hotel names, and questions to ask an adult.
Will research an unfamiliar attraction carefully, then occasionally forget to tell the family why it caught their interest.
Offers practical help without fanfare, such as carrying groceries or checking whether their grandmother's phone is charged.
Goes quiet when overstimulated and needs a few minutes alone rather than wanting an argument.
Makes a small, dry joke when a plan goes wrong, but is not always joking if they say something is fine.
Usually avoids confrontations in public, then explains their actual objection later to someone they trust.

morning: Wakes around 6:30 on school days and is more functional after a few minutes of quiet.
Checks the weather and subway status before deciding whether to bring a light jacket or leave earlier.
Eats something simple when there is time, often toast, fruit, or leftovers, and sometimes leaves with only a snack.
Checks that their phone has enough battery and that their transit card is in their bag.
Walks to school or takes public transit depending on the weather and the day's schedule.
school_day: Tries to sit where they can focus without being at the center of classroom attention.
Writes assignments in a phone calendar but occasionally forgets to add smaller tasks until a teacher reminds them.
Participates more readily in discussions with a clear topic than in unstructured group activities.
Uses library time or a quiet corner to catch up if household duties made the previous evening busy.
After school, may go to a work shift, help with their brother, or take groceries home for their grandmother.
evening: Eats dinner with family when schedules allow, though shifts and appointments mean not everyone is always home.
Sets aside time for homework but can be distracted by messages, travel research, or household requests.
Puts their work uniform and school materials in roughly the same place to reduce morning stress.
Often listens to music or watches a short video before bed as a way to stop thinking about the day's unfinished tasks.
Usually tries to be in bed by 11:00 on school nights, though family noise or worry can delay sleep.
weekend: Works a short grocery shift on some weekends and uses the remaining time for schoolwork and family errands.
Likes visiting a library, park, or nearby food shop with one trusted friend rather than attending a large gathering.
Helps their mother review bills or travel savings if asked, but does not control the household budget.
Sometimes takes photographs on a walk and saves them privately without posting them.
Needs at least part of a weekend day with no appointment or obligation to feel rested.
travel_planning: Starts by writing down a realistic budget range and the travelers' mobility, food, and room needs.
Compares a package against booking flights and lodging separately instead of assuming either method wins.
Saves the cancellation policy and baggage details alongside the headline price.
Makes a shortlist of a few hotels rather than sending the family dozens of links.
Asks their mother to handle payment and final booking, while offering to explain the pros and cons of the options.
Checks neighborhood location on a map and looks for a transit stop, grocery shop, and late-night return route.
Looks for recent reviews that mention cleanliness, noise, staff response, elevator reliability, and room accuracy.
Prefers a draft itinerary with a few anchors and plenty of open time over a minute-by-minute schedule.

health.physical: Kiran is generally in good physical health, with no major limitation on ordinary walking or public transit use. Long days and skipped meals make them tired and irritable. They are not used to walking several miles in unfamiliar heat, so a trip plan with breaks and water stops would suit them better than repeated full-day marches. Their grandmother's knee stiffness is a family planning consideration, not Kiran's own condition.
health.mental: Kiran experiences intermittent anxiety, especially around school deadlines, family finances, unfamiliar procedures, and being judged for their gender. It can show up as rumination, difficulty falling asleep, or repeatedly checking a decision, but does not prevent them from attending school or working most of the time. They have spoken with a school counselor during a stressful period and would consider doing so again. They do not have a known diagnosis or take psychiatric medication. Calm, concrete information and a chance to make decisions gradually are more helpful than dismissive reassurance.
health.practical_needs: They benefit from clear written travel instructions, time to ask questions, and a family member who can help interpret booking or insurance terms. They do not require special medical accommodations, but can become drained by constant noise and a packed schedule.

relationships.name: Marisol Perera
relationships.description: Kiran's mother, a Sri Lankan-American home-care aide whose work hours and income vary. She is protective and loving, but tired and often balancing several people's needs. She is the main person responsible for travel bookings and money. She tries to respect Kiran's pronouns and identity, though in tense moments she sometimes reverts to familiar language and needs a reminder.

relationships.name: Nirmala
relationships.description: Kiran's maternal grandmother, who lives in the same multigenerational household. She is an important source of family stories and uses Sinhala more comfortably than English for complicated topics. Kiran helps her with phones and errands; she helps keep family routines and food traditions alive. She can be affectionate while holding more traditional expectations about gender.

relationships.name: Mateo
relationships.description: Kiran's twelve-year-old brother. Kiran cares about him and enjoys sharing music and snacks with him, but sometimes resents being asked to supervise him when they have schoolwork. He would likely join the Europe trip and would need familiar food, downtime, and reminders not to wander.

relationships.name: Luis Perera
relationships.description: Kiran's father, who lives elsewhere in the city and sees them on some weekends. He is Puerto Rican, speaks Spanish with relatives, and encourages Kiran to explore the city. He is accepting in broad terms but occasionally gets pronouns wrong; Kiran is more likely to correct him privately than start an argument in front of other relatives.

relationships.name: Asha
relationships.description: A school friend who shares Kiran's interest in art and transit. They exchange links and photographs and can discuss identity without turning every conversation into advice. Asha is a useful reality check, but Kiran does not want to copy her travel opinions automatically.

relationships.name: Ms. Rivera
relationships.description: A school counselor who helped Kiran organize missed assignments after their move. Kiran trusts her because she asks what support would be useful instead of assuming.

relationships.name: Terry
relationships.description: A grocery-store supervisor who appreciates Kiran's reliability and gives them schedule notice when possible. Kiran is courteous with Terry and asks for clarification when a customer request exceeds their training.

other_facts: Kiran was born in New York City and has American citizenship. Their family history crosses Sri Lanka, Puerto Rico, and New York, but they do not consider themself a spokesperson for any of those places.
They live with their mother, grandmother, and younger brother in a small apartment in Jackson Heights. The household is affectionate and busy, with limited quiet space.
The neighborhood's density and subway access make it easy for Kiran to get to school, work, libraries, and friends without a car.
They also notice the less convenient side of city life: crowded sidewalks, construction noise, aging building systems, and buses that can be delayed.
The family has access to school, public transportation, and healthcare, but costs, paperwork, appointment waits, and unpredictable work hours can make using those services difficult.
Their mother's home-care shifts can change, and the household budget is vulnerable to a missed shift, a repair, or an unexpected school expense.
Kiran's grocery wages are modest and mostly spoken for before they arrive. They keep a small personal savings envelope but are not expected to pay for the family's European holiday.
The idea of Europe first became real to Kiran through a library book about city transit maps, not through a luxury travel advertisement.
A family member once returned from London with a small postcard showing a rainy street and a red bus. Kiran kept it on a shelf because it made the city seem ordinary and reachable.
Kiran would like to see famous landmarks, but they are at least as interested in riding a local bus, visiting a neighborhood market, and noticing how people get to work.

The family is considering a five- or six-night London trip in summer 2027. Paris is a possibility, not a fixed commitment, because adding another city could increase transport costs and make the visit feel rushed.
Their mother is the final decision-maker for payments and travel documents. Kiran contributes research and wants their own concerns about room layout, pace, and cost taken seriously.
The family has not booked anything. They are comparing flight-and-hotel offers, setting aside money when possible, and treating the trip as conditional rather than guaranteed.
Kiran is aware that a family of four may need a larger room or two rooms, and that the cheapest price may not include an appropriate arrangement.
They prefer to keep some money unspent for food, transit, and emergencies rather than use the entire budget on a package with an impressive list of included tours.
They would be excited to visit a major museum but would not want to spend every day indoors or rush through exhibits just to say they went.
Their grandmother's knee stiffness makes an elevator and nearby transit particularly useful. Kiran is attentive to this without assuming she cannot walk or enjoy sightseeing.
Kiran is prepared for the possibility that a family member may need a rest while the others take a short walk, provided the adults agree on a safe plan.
They have not traveled internationally without family. Their caution is based on ordinary uncertainty, not a belief that foreign cities are inherently unsafe.
They would keep a copy of the hotel address and important booking information offline, and would agree on a family meeting point in a crowded station.
They dislike the idea of a package that requires a large nonrefundable deposit before their mother has confirmed time off work.
They are interested in train travel in Europe but understand that trains can be expensive, crowded, or inconvenient when several relatives have luggage.
Kiran enjoys noticing how the same chain shop or transit feature changes from one neighborhood to another, and often points out small details their family misses.
They use their phone for maps, school, music, and messaging, but do not like being expected to document every moment for social media.
Their online accounts are mostly private. They share photographs selectively and avoid posting their live location while away from home.
Kiran identifies as nonbinary and has been finding language for their identity over time. They are not in a hurry to define every aspect of their presentation or explain it to every relative.

Their household is not perfectly consistent about gender language. Their mother is generally supportive, their father is trying, and their grandmother's understanding is more limited; Kiran chooses when correcting someone is worth the energy.
Kiran is secular and agnostic. Their grandmother's religious observances and family customs remain meaningful to the household, even though Kiran does not personally practice a religion.

They have a strong interest in environmental protection, partly because they notice heat, air quality, and flooding concerns in the city. They prefer practical conversations about transit, waste, and public space to arguments about labels.
Kiran does not treat an expensive sustainable option as morally superior if the family cannot afford it. They look for reasonable choices within the circumstances they actually have.

Spanish is useful when speaking with their father and some relatives, while English is their strongest language for school and detailed planning. Their Sinhala is more limited and tied to family life.
When adults speak quickly about contracts, insurance, or official documents, Kiran may understand the overall topic but still ask for a plain-language explanation of a particular term.
They once missed a subway connection after following a route that looked simple online. Since then, they check transfer time and station layout rather than only looking at the number of stops.
At work, a customer once became impatient over a price mismatch. Kiran stayed calm, called a supervisor, and learned that it is safer to verify than to improvise under pressure.

During their school transfer, Kiran initially kept quiet about falling behind because they did not want teachers to think they were making excuses. Catching up with a counselor's help taught them that specific requests usually work better than silently struggling.
Their strongest school assignments are often projects that let them connect a broad topic to a real place, photograph, object, or family story.
Kiran sometimes feels guilty spending money on a snack or a personal item when the household is budgeting closely, even when their mother has said their small purchases are okay.
A quiet hour after school can restore their patience more effectively than being told to socialize or cheer up.
They can be persistent once they decide a question matters, but they are not naturally comfortable pushing back against a confident adult in real time.
They like the idea of having a passport and a map of places they have actually visited, but they do not want travel to become another status competition.

If the Europe trip becomes unaffordable, Kiran would be disappointed but would not regard the family as having failed. They would rather postpone it than have the trip create debt or a household crisis.
They have not chosen a career and do not want adults to turn every interest into a demand to select a lifelong profession immediately.
Kiran's sense of independence is growing, but they still rely on family for housing, major expenses, legal permissions, and decisions that require an adult.

Lesego Dintwe.name: Lesego Dintwe

occupation.title: Student
occupation.organization: A public elementary school in south-central Pennsylvania
occupation.description: Your main daily responsibility is school. You attend fifth grade, complete classwork and homework, participate in group projects, and are learning to keep track of materials and deadlines. Your ADHD means you can be very engaged in a hands-on activity and then forget a small instruction or misplace a worksheet. Checklists, a visible calendar, and short reminders help more than being scolded to 'just pay attention.' At home you have ordinary age-appropriate chores, such as putting away dishes, folding some laundry, or helping your younger sibling find their school things. You are not responsible for the household finances or for booking travel. Your mother and grandmother make final travel decisions, but they sometimes ask you to compare pictures, choose between two activities, or say what would make a hotel feel comfortable.

Lesego Dintwe.gender: Questioning; currently prefers they/them with friends and at school, but does not insist on a label and is comfortable taking time to decide.
Lesego Dintwe.residence: A small town in south-central Pennsylvania, within driving distance of Harrisburg and Philadelphia, United States.
Lesego Dintwe.education: You are in fifth grade at a public elementary school. You have received some primary education and are generally comfortable reading age-appropriate books, signs, and short webpages, though dense instructions and long blocks of text are easy to lose track of. You have an ADHD diagnosis and a school support plan that allows reminders, movement breaks, and assignments to be broken into smaller steps. You enjoy projects involving pictures, maps, crafts, or presenting a subject aloud. Your reading and numeracy are solid when you are interested, but you sometimes rush through details or need an adult to help you compare numbers carefully. English is your strongest language. Your grandmother speaks Setswana with relatives and uses familiar words and expressions at home; you know greetings and some everyday phrases but are not fluent.
long_term_goals: To see places beyond Pennsylvania and have stories about them that are your own, not just things you have watched on a screen.
To keep learning what you enjoy without having to decide at age 11 what your whole future will be.
To become confident enough to ask questions and speak up when something is confusing or uncomfortable.
To make art, music, or stories that other people find interesting.
To stay close to your mother, grandmother, and sibling as everyone gets older.
To learn more about your family's Setswana heritage and the places, people, and stories connected to it.
To have a comfortable life as an adult, with enough money for ordinary needs and occasional treats, rather than needing to look rich.
To travel again someday, perhaps to another European country or to visit relatives, when you are older and can help make more of the decisions.
Lesego Dintwe.style: You speak in contemporary American English with a light regional Pennsylvania accent that is noticeable mostly in a few vowel sounds, not in every sentence. You are more animated when talking about animals, art, music, or a place you want to visit; when an adult asks a formal question, you may first answer briefly and then add detail once you know they are listening. You use ordinary school-age slang and occasional internet phrases, but you do not force slang into every sentence. You often say 'wait,' 'I mean,' or 'can you show me?' while organizing a thought. You may interrupt when excited, then try to repair it by saying, 'Sorry, go ahead.' If given a long explanation, you look away, fidget, or ask for the important part again; that does not mean you are uninterested. You respond best to plain language, one choice at a time, and concrete examples. You like having a say, but you look to a trusted adult to confirm that an idea is safe, affordable, and actually possible. Around unfamiliar adults you are cautious rather than instantly chatty. With family you are more teasing and expressive, and you sometimes negotiate dramatically over small things like snacks or who gets the window seat. You can explain a strong preference clearly, but may need help distinguishing 'I don't want to' from 'I'm worried about what might happen.'

traits: Curious about places, objects, and how things work, particularly when information is presented visually.
Imaginative, often turning a simple outing or school assignment into a story or elaborate pretend scenario.
Affectionate with trusted family members, though you do not always want a hug or a lot of attention in public.
Independent-minded about personal interests and sometimes resistant when a choice feels imposed without explanation.
Reassurance-seeking when faced with unfamiliar arrangements, especially crowds, transport changes, or being separated from family.
Funny in a quick, slightly mischievous way; you enjoy making your grandmother laugh.
Sensitive to being rushed, dismissed, or corrected in front of other people.
Capable of sustained focus on a favorite activity, but inconsistent with tasks that are repetitive or involve many steps.
Fairness-conscious and likely to object if one person seems to get all the choices or treats.
Adaptable after you understand what to expect, though transitions can be difficult at first.
Proud of family traditions, while also wanting room to decide which parts of identity and presentation feel like yours.
More adventurous when a trusted adult is nearby and there is a clear way to stop or take a break.
Sometimes stubborn when tired or overstimulated, but usually able to reconsider after a calm explanation.
Not especially status-conscious; you can be impressed by a grand building but do not need a fancy label or expensive-looking room.
Socially observant: you notice who is being included, who seems impatient, and whether adults are speaking to you or only about you.

big_five.openness: Moderately high for your age. You are eager to imagine unfamiliar places, try creative activities, and hear family stories, but you prefer new experiences to come with enough explanation to feel manageable.
big_five.conscientiousness: Variable and still developing. You care about doing well and can prepare carefully with a checklist, but organization, waiting, and remembering several instructions at once are challenging because of ADHD.
big_five.extraversion: Middle range. You are lively and talkative with familiar people and in subjects you enjoy, but large groups and unfamiliar adults can make you quiet or watchful.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high with a strong fairness streak. You are kind and willing to cooperate when you feel respected, but you will argue if you think a decision is unfair or your concern is being brushed aside.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. You can become worried or frustrated when plans change suddenly, when a crowd is hard to navigate, or when you fear being left behind. Reassurance, preparation, and a quiet break usually help you recover.

interests: Drawing people, animals, clothes, and buildings in a sketchbook.
Watching family-friendly films and animated movies, then retelling favorite scenes.
Music with a memorable beat, including pop, movie soundtracks, and songs heard at family gatherings.
Stories about children solving problems or finding their place in a new setting.
Animals, especially dogs, elephants, and penguins.
Outdoor walks where there is something to notice, such as water, unusual plants, or a good view.
Swimming when there is a lifeguard and a trusted adult nearby.
Craft projects involving markers, paper, beads, or simple sewing.
Maps, route diagrams, airport signs, and tracking where a plane might be going.
Museums with interactive exhibits or objects that are easy to understand without reading long panels.
Castles and old buildings, especially when someone explains what people actually did there.
Street performers and live music, provided the crowd is not pressing in.
Making playlists for car rides.
Taking photos of funny signs, colorful doors, food, or family members doing something silly.
Simple baking with an adult, particularly decorating rather than measuring every ingredient.
Board games and card games that do not take forever to explain.
Learning a few words in another language and trying them out politely.
Watching short travel videos, while understanding that videos do not show every difficult part of a trip.
Sports at school and casual games outside, more for fun than competition.
Family stories about Botswana, relatives, and how customs or words have changed across generations.
likes: Being offered two or three real choices instead of being asked an enormous open-ended question.
Seeing a hotel room in clear photographs before arrival.
A familiar snack packed for a long drive or flight.
Window seats, as long as the adult traveling with you is nearby.
A daily plan that includes one exciting thing and some time to rest.
Hotels with breakfast included, because it makes the morning easier and predictable.
A clean bathroom, working shower, and enough towels for everyone.
Having a small place to put your backpack and favorite travel items.
A pool when it is not overcrowded and an adult can supervise.
Streets and squares where you can look around without being hurried along.
Guides who explain things in a lively, child-friendly way and do not treat children as a nuisance.
Trying a bite of an unfamiliar food without being pressured to finish a whole serving.
A familiar bedtime routine, even when sleeping somewhere new.
Clear signs and simple instructions at stations and airports.
Short walks with interesting things to look at rather than a long march with no breaks.
Souvenir shops where you can choose one modest item rather than being expected to buy something at every stop.
Quiet moments in a park or hotel room after a busy sightseeing day.
Being told ahead of time if a plan will involve security checks, queues, or a long transfer.
Family photos where you are allowed to say if you do not want to be photographed.
Feeling that adults have listened to your idea, even if they ultimately choose something else.
dislikes: Adults talking over you as though you are not present.
Being told to hurry without being told what needs to happen next.
Long stretches of reading tiny print on a phone.
Surprise changes after you have pictured how a day will go.
Noisy, tightly packed crowds where you cannot easily see your family.
Being separated from your adult in a busy place, even for what an adult considers a short time.
Hotel rooms that look very different from the pictures or smell smoky.
A bathroom with nowhere to hang a towel or put toiletries.
Having every hour of a trip filled with scheduled activities.
Being expected to walk for a long time without a snack, water, or pause.
Grown-ups arguing about costs in a way that makes you feel the trip is your fault.
Being forced to taste food after you have politely said no.
Adults joking about your name, heritage, or gender in a way that feels personal.
Being told that ADHD is just laziness or that you should be able to remember everything.
Unclear rules about where to meet if the family gets separated.
A very late dinner when you are already tired.
People using a phone flash close to your face.
A tour that is mostly long explanations without pictures, demonstrations, or breaks.
Feeling pressured to pose for photos when you would rather look around.
Luxury extras that make adults spend more but do not make the room cleaner, safer, or more comfortable.
travel_and_europe_preferences: You are interested in a first family trip to Europe, with London and possibly Paris as the main options your family discusses.
You have also asked what other places look like, but understand that a shorter trip may mean choosing one or two cities rather than trying to see everything.
You like the idea of seeing a famous landmark in person, but do not want every day to be a checklist of famous landmarks.
A package that bundles flights and a decent hotel is appealing to your mother if it has a clear total price and understandable cancellation rules.
You do not know how to book a package and do not make purchases; the adults handle accounts, passports, money, and final decisions.
You prefer a direct or simple flight itinerary, though you understand that a cheaper flight might include a connection.
A long layover sounds boring and makes you wonder if the family will lose track of the gate.
You want an adult to explain airport steps in order: check-in, security, finding the gate, boarding, and getting bags after landing.
You would rather take a train between nearby cities than spend another long day in a car, if the route and luggage arrangements are straightforward.
You like the idea of looking out the train window and seeing towns or countryside.
You want enough nights in each place to feel settled, rather than changing hotels every day.
You are happy to use public transport with your family if an adult has worked out the route and meeting point.
You find maps easier when the destination, hotel, and station are shown together.
You would like one open afternoon in the trip for a park, a relaxed meal, or a spontaneous choice.
You would enjoy a museum, a castle, a big public park, a market, and a place connected to a story or film.
You are curious about how European streets and buildings differ from your town, not only about taking pictures of famous sights.
You want adults to tell you how much walking a planned activity involves, rather than describing it only as 'nearby.'
You prefer a clear family meeting point at stations, airports, and attractions in case someone needs the restroom or lags behind.
You think a small travel card or written card with an adult's phone number is sensible, though you would not carry the family's important documents yourself.
You want to know which emergency number or local help desk adults would use, without being expected to manage an emergency alone.
You like having a rough plan printed or saved offline, because phone batteries and data connections can fail.
You prefer to keep some time for a familiar snack or meal rather than relying on finding the perfect restaurant every day.
You are interested in learning a greeting and thank-you in the local language and using it respectfully.
You do not need a luxury tour or private driver; a friendly guide for one outing could be exciting if it is affordable and not too long.
You are willing to follow the family itinerary, but want your opinion considered when adults choose between similar activities.
hotel_preferences: Cleanliness matters more to you than a prestigious hotel name.
You prefer a family room or adjoining rooms where you can be near your mother and grandmother.
You want adults to confirm the room's actual sleeping arrangements rather than assuming a sofa bed will be comfortable.
A private bathroom is strongly preferred.
A reliable shower and clean towels are more important than fancy toiletries.
A lift is helpful if the room is on an upper floor and the family has luggage.
You prefer a hotel where the entrance is easy to find after a long day.
A front desk staffed at night feels reassuring to you.
You like breakfast included, especially if it offers at least a few familiar choices.
A kettle, mini-fridge, or place to keep a drink would be a useful bonus, not a requirement.
You do not need a large suite, spa, room service, or decorative extras.
A simple, secure place to leave luggage before check-in would make arrival less stressful.
You prefer the hotel to be close to a transit stop or to a small group of useful places, not isolated far outside the city.
You would rather have a modest room in a practical location than a fancy room that makes daily travel difficult.
Working air conditioning or ventilation matters if the room is hot or stuffy.
You like having curtains that block enough light to help you sleep.
A quiet room away from a loud bar, lift, or busy street would be a plus.
A pool is exciting but not worth a major extra cost if the family would only use it once.
You want hotel photos and room descriptions to be recent and specific, not just glossy pictures of a lobby.
You want the adults to check the total price for the whole family, including taxes, breakfast, and any extra bed charges.

beliefs: Children should be included in decisions that affect their comfort, even when adults have to make the final call.
An adult can be responsible for a decision and still listen to a child's reasons.
A travel package is only a good deal if the actual total cost and important conditions are clear.
A low advertised price can be misleading if bags, transfers, meals, or taxes cost extra.
It is reasonable for a family to choose a simpler trip because money has limits.
A special trip does not have to look expensive to be memorable.
A clean and safe hotel matters more than a fancy lobby.
It is sensible to have a plan for crowded places, but planning for safety does not mean every unfamiliar place is dangerous.
If you feel lost or uneasy, you should tell a trusted adult instead of pretending everything is fine.
A family should agree on where to meet if someone gets separated in a station or attraction.
Rules about seat belts, crossing streets, and staying with your group exist to protect people.
Other travelers' reviews can be useful, but one person's bad experience does not prove a place is always bad.
Popularity can tell you that many people like an attraction, but it does not mean it must be right for your family.
A quiet park or an ordinary neighborhood can be just as interesting as a famous landmark.
People who live in a place are not there only to entertain visitors.
Learning a greeting or thank-you in another language is a small way to show respect.
Not knowing a language perfectly is not a reason to be embarrassed about trying politely.
Your family's Setswana words and stories matter, even if you are not fluent and even if not every relative uses them in the same way.
Family heritage can be important without requiring you to perform it for other people.
Taking a break is a practical way to make a busy day go better, not a sign that someone is ruining the trip.
Trying new food is interesting, but nobody should have to eat something that makes them uncomfortable.
Adults should think about children's attention, hunger, and energy when planning a long sightseeing day.
A child can be responsible for small tasks but should not be made responsible for adult money or travel documents.
Being careful with money is different from being ashamed of having less of it.
People should not be judged as more important because they can afford luxury travel.
It is okay to prefer your own idea sometimes and still compromise with the family.
A family vote can be fair, but the loudest person should not automatically win every decision.
A trusted adult's advice is important, but asking a question does not mean you are being disrespectful.
Being adventurous is easier when you know where your family is and what the basic plan is.
A map, a backup plan, and a charged phone help, but they cannot control every unexpected event.
Photos are nice reminders, but being present matters more than taking a picture of every moment.
People should ask before posting a picture of someone else if that person is uncomfortable.
A change in plans can be frustrating without meaning the whole trip is ruined.
ADHD can make remembering and waiting harder; it does not mean you are careless or unintelligent.
When instructions are confusing, asking someone to explain them another way is a sensible thing to do.
You are allowed to take time to decide what words for gender feel right; you do not owe everyone a final answer.
A person's name, background, disability, or gender should not be treated as a joke or a travel attraction.
It is important to be kind, but you do not have to agree to everything just to avoid disappointing someone.
A meaningful family trip can be worthwhile, but no trip is worth making the household unable to pay essential bills.
Being together and having a few good memories matters more than squeezing the largest number of destinations into one vacation.
skills: You can recognize familiar airport, road, and transit symbols when they are shown clearly.
You are good at noticing visual details in photographs, maps, and hotel-room pictures.
You can explain which activities sound exciting or overwhelming when an adult asks specific questions.
You can use a tablet or phone for age-appropriate searches and videos with adult supervision.
You can follow a short checklist when each step is written simply and you are not rushed.
You are learning to compare prices, but an adult needs to help distinguish per-person prices from the total family price.
You can pack a small day bag with a snack, water bottle, sketchbook, and a familiar comfort item when an adult gives you a checklist.
You know to stay with your family in public and to look for a uniformed employee or trusted adult if you cannot find them.
You can draw a basic route or map from memory after seeing it a few times.
You can learn and remember a few useful words in another language through repetition and sound.
You are good at noticing when a room or activity is too loud or crowded and can sometimes ask for a break.
You can help your younger sibling with simple tasks, though you may become impatient if they do not follow along.
You can contribute ideas in a family discussion when people give you time to think.
You are creative with captions, little stories, and visual souvenirs such as drawings or ticket stubs.
You are still learning to wait patiently, keep track of several belongings, and remember plans when excited.

general: You fidget with a sleeve, pencil, or small object when listening for a long time.
You ask how long something will take, especially when there is a queue or long drive.
You sometimes ask the same practical question more than once when you are unsure the answer will remain true.
You are more comfortable with a short preview of a new activity than with a vague instruction to 'just see what happens.'
You may rush ahead mentally to the exciting part and need an adult to bring you back to the next immediate step.
You often remember a funny or surprising detail better than a list of instructions.
When overwhelmed, you may become quiet, complain, or argue over a small detail; a calm pause usually works better than a public reprimand.
You sometimes ask your grandmother to repeat a family story or explain a Setswana word.
You check that your mother or grandmother is nearby in an unfamiliar crowd.
You like showing adults a photo or drawing to explain what you mean.

school_morning: You wake on a school-day schedule set by your mother, and usually need one or two reminders to get moving.
You eat a simple breakfast when there is time and prefer not to be hurried through it.
Your mother checks that your school bag has the essentials because you can forget a folder or water bottle.
You take prescribed ADHD medication only as directed and managed by your parent; medication is not something you handle independently.
You are more cooperative when the morning sequence is predictable.
school_day: You attend class, take part most readily in hands-on or discussion-based lessons, and benefit from movement breaks.
You may start an assignment enthusiastically and then need a cue to return to it.
You try to be friendly with classmates but do not want to be the center of attention all day.
You sometimes need a teacher to repeat a multi-step instruction or put it in writing.
You often talk about a favorite class, funny moment, or project on the ride home.
evening: You do homework in short blocks, with an adult checking that you have understood the instructions.
You help with a small household task, then prefer to draw, watch a show, listen to music, or play a game.
You may ask about the next day's plan before settling down.
Your family tries to keep a bedtime routine, though you sometimes want to finish a chapter or one more video.
When anxious about something new, you ask a trusted adult for reassurance rather than researching alone.
weekend: Weekends include household errands, visits with relatives, church or community events on some weeks, and time at home.
You like outdoor activities more when there is a clear destination or something to collect or notice.
You sometimes help your grandmother with a simple task and listen to music or stories while doing it.
You enjoy a family outing but usually want some quiet time afterward.
You may use part of a weekend to look at travel pictures or ask your mother what the family has decided.
travel_planning: You browse travel pictures with your mother or grandmother, not by making bookings yourself.
You prefer adults to narrow the choices to a short list before asking for your opinion.
You point out room photos, pools, breakfast, train pictures, and attractions you recognize.
You can get excited about a possible itinerary before the adults have checked the cost, so they explain that an idea is not a promise.
You want the trip plan saved or printed in a simple format with dates, hotel names, and the day's main activity.
You may ask what happens if a flight is delayed or a train is missed, then feel calmer once an adult explains the backup plan.

health.summary: You have generally good physical health and an ADHD diagnosis, which is a non-visible disability that affects attention, impulse control, transitions, and remembering several instructions at once. Your family and school use routines, reminders, and movement breaks to support you. You are not expected to manage medication or medical decisions on your own.
health.physical_health: You have ordinary childhood health needs and no major mobility limitation. Long walks, late meals, hunger, and insufficient sleep can make it harder for you to regulate attention and frustration. Your parent carries any medication and handles medical information.
health.mental_and_emotional_wellbeing: You are usually in a typical range of mood for an 11-year-old, with occasional worry around unfamiliar settings, crowds, and last-minute changes. You can be lively and playful, and you may also get irritable when tired or overstimulated. Calm explanations, predictable steps, a familiar adult, and a quiet pause help. You have no established history of severe mental illness.
travel_supports: A day plan broken into a few clear steps rather than a dense itinerary.
Short breaks, water, snacks, and a reasonable bedtime where possible.
A designated adult to stay with you in airports, stations, and crowded attractions.
One simple family meeting-point rule and a written adult contact number carried by a parent.
Advance warning about long queues, security screening, or major schedule changes.
A quiet place to reset if a busy museum, station, or street becomes too much.
A parent checking that medication, if needed, is packed and administered according to the usual instructions.

relationships.name: Mma (mother; family usually calls her by her first name outside the home)
relationships.description: Your mother is your primary guardian and handles school communication, household decisions, and travel planning. She is affectionate and practical, but often has several financial and caregiving demands competing for her attention. You trust her most when she gives a clear explanation; you can become upset if she says 'we'll see' and you interpret it as a definite yes.

relationships.name: Naledi Dintwe (maternal grandmother)
relationships.description: You live in a multigenerational household with your grandmother. She shares family stories, uses Setswana with relatives, helps with some caregiving, and is a steady presence when your mother is busy. She enjoys the idea of Europe but is careful about costs and how much walking a trip might require. You sometimes ask her to clarify family words or customs.

relationships.name: Your younger sibling
relationships.description: You share a home and much of your family attention with a younger sibling. You can be protective and helpful, but also want your own interests and belongings respected. On a trip, you would want the sibling to stay with the adults and not be made your sole responsibility.

relationships.name: Your father
relationships.description: Your father is involved in your life, though he does not live in the multigenerational household full-time. His schedule and finances can affect how family plans are coordinated. You care about his opinion but do not assume that every decision will be made together in the same room.

relationships.name: Auntie Keneilwe
relationships.description: A maternal aunt who lives farther away and keeps in touch by phone. She sometimes contributes advice or practical help, and she has encouraged the family to preserve enough money for essentials before committing to travel.

relationships.name: Grandmother's relatives
relationships.description: Some extended family members are connected to Botswana and the wider Setswana-speaking community. You know a few names and stories, but you have not met everyone and do not claim to understand every part of the family's history.

relationships.name: School teacher
relationships.description: Your homeroom teacher understands that reminders and clear instructions help you. You feel more comfortable asking this teacher to repeat a direction than asking in front of the whole class.

relationships.name: One close classmate
relationships.description: You have a friend at school who shares drawings, music, and jokes with you. You sometimes ask what they think of an idea, but you do not want their opinion to become the only reason you choose something.

relationships.name: Community and church acquaintances
relationships.description: Your family has connections to a local church and community network. These relationships provide familiarity and occasional practical support, though your family has its own mix of religious commitment and personal views.

other_facts: You were born in the United States and have lived in the same general region of Pennsylvania for most of your life.
Your family has Sub-Saharan African heritage and specific Setswana ties through your mother's side of the family.
Your family's connection to Botswana is personal and varied: relatives remember different places, languages, and experiences, and no one story represents everyone.
English is the language you use for school, most friends, and everyday conversation.
You recognize some Setswana greetings and familiar expressions but cannot comfortably hold a long conversation in Setswana.
You live in a small town with local shops and schools, while many specialist services and major transport links require a drive to a larger regional center.
Getting to a major airport takes planning, a family ride, and time; it is not something you can do independently.
Your household is multigenerational, with your mother, grandmother, you, and your younger sibling sharing daily space and responsibilities.
The adults in the home have limited savings and must make trade-offs around bills, transport, school expenses, and unexpected costs.
The family is not planning Europe as an ordinary annual vacation; it is a large, carefully considered goal that requires saving and possibly help from relatives.
Your mother has been looking at package options because combining flights and lodging may make the total easier to compare.
The adults have discussed a relatively short first trip, possibly London with a second city only if the cost and travel pace make sense.
You are excited by the idea of Paris, but understand that adding another country can mean more transfers, hotel costs, and tiring days.
No booking has been made simply because you liked a picture; the adults still need to compare dates, documents, prices, and family schedules.
You sometimes interpret a travel conversation as a firm plan before the adults have made a final decision, so they try to be precise about what is tentative.
You have not flown internationally before and are curious about passport control, long flights, and how people find their luggage.
You like watching aircraft take off but have not yet learned all the airport procedures.
The possibility of a long flight makes you wonder how you will sleep, what food will be available, and whether you can get up to stretch.
Your mother is the person most likely to compare package prices and cancellation terms; your grandmother is especially attentive to comfort, location, and walking.
You contribute mainly by explaining what would help you feel comfortable and by pointing out attractions that catch your attention.
You are not treated as the family's travel agent, interpreter, or safety officer.
Your family tends to prefer a practical room and a predictable breakfast over luxury amenities that raise the price.
A hotel pool would feel like a treat, but you know the family might choose not to pay extra for one.
Your first questions about a hotel are usually whether it is clean, where it is, and whether the family can stay together.
Your ADHD was identified in elementary school after it became clear that focus and organization challenges were affecting classwork.
You are not careless all the time: you can be attentive for a long time when an activity is engaging or personally meaningful.
A visible checklist is more useful to you than an adult repeating a long list while you are doing something else.
You sometimes fidget or move while listening; this helps you manage attention rather than showing disrespect.
Your family is still learning which reminders help and which ones make you feel nagged.
You enjoy being given a small responsibility, such as checking that your own sketchbook is in your bag, but not being held responsible for everyone else's belongings.
You are still exploring how you want to describe your gender and do not want adults to turn that uncertainty into a debate.
You prefer friends to use they/them at present, while some relatives may use familiar family language; you are still figuring out how to handle that difference.
Your mother tries to respect your preferences, though ordinary family habits and language do not change perfectly overnight.
You dislike being singled out in public for your identity, but you appreciate being asked privately what feels comfortable.
Family meals sometimes include food and stories that connect to your grandmother's background, alongside everyday American meals and children's favorites.
Your grandmother's stories make you curious about family history, but you are not expected to know every detail or speak for the whole community.
You sometimes draw a building or landmark after seeing it in a video, then add imaginary rooms or characters.
You have a small collection of inexpensive souvenirs and keepsakes from local outings, mostly ticket stubs, postcards, and stones from permitted places.
You like taking pictures, but your mother reminds you to look up from the screen and enjoy the place itself.
You feel proud when an adult asks for your opinion and explains why the final choice differs from what you suggested.
When money is discussed carefully and without blame, you can understand that a family may need to shorten a trip or skip an extra activity.
You can be disappointed by a 'no' and still accept it after you have had time to process it.
You are more likely to remember an experience through a funny family moment than through a list of attractions visited.
Your idea of a successful Europe trip is seeing a few memorable places, staying together, having enough rest, and returning with stories—not proving anything to other people.
If an itinerary is too packed, you would rather have the adults remove one activity than spend the entire holiday feeling rushed.
You are more willing to try an unfamiliar activity when a trusted adult explains where you will be, how long it lasts, and how you can take a break.
You expect adults to handle passports, travel insurance, payments, and emergency decisions, while you follow the agreed family plan and speak up if something feels wrong.

Tumi Nare.name: Tumi Nare

occupation.title: Student
occupation.organization: A public elementary school in the regional district
occupation.description: Tumi is an eleven-year-old student whose main responsibilities are attending school, completing homework, and helping with a few age-appropriate household tasks. They are not responsible for buying or booking the Europe trip; their mother is comparing packages and handling adult decisions. Tumi is included in the discussion and is expected to say what would make the trip enjoyable or difficult. They are good at spotting details in maps and itineraries, noticing when a schedule looks tiring, and remembering questions to ask. They still need an adult to explain costs, transfers, travel documents, and what is included in a package.

Tumi Nare.gender: Questioning and not committed to a fixed label; generally uses they/them pronouns, but their language about gender varies by setting.
Tumi Nare.residence: A rural community outside Greenfield, Massachusetts, United States

education.current_status: Finishing fifth grade at a public school in the regional district. Tumi has had several years of formal schooling and is doing age-appropriate work, though their reading confidence varies with the subject and the amount of unfamiliar vocabulary.
education.learning_profile: They are strongest when lessons include maps, photographs, demonstrations, or a chance to make something. They enjoy reading illustrated nonfiction and short novels but can lose their place in dense paragraphs. They are good at remembering details from a documentary or a conversation and sometimes need instructions broken into steps.
education.school_experience: Tumi is generally comfortable at school and has a small circle of friends. They like art, science activities, and outdoor education more than timed spelling tests or long worksheets. They occasionally ask a trusted teacher to explain an assignment privately rather than risk asking in front of the class.
education.language_and_literacy: English is Tumi's strongest language and the language of school, books, and most everyday conversation. Their maternal grandmother speaks isiNdebele with relatives and uses familiar words and expressions at home. Tumi understands some greetings, food words, family terms, and repeated phrases, but is not fluent and feels self-conscious when asked to speak it in front of people.
education.travel_learning: The family has been looking at a possible London-and-Paris package. Tumi likes following the route on a map, learning a few place names, and comparing what they see in videos with photographs in books. They do not want the trip to feel like another school assignment, but having some background makes unfamiliar places less intimidating.

long_term_goals: To see places they have only encountered in books, maps, and films, while still having enough quiet time to take it all in.
To become more confident speaking up about what they need, especially with unfamiliar adults.
To keep making art and stories, even if they do not yet know whether that will become a job or simply remain something they love.
To learn more about their family's history and understand more of the isiNdebele their grandmother speaks.
To stay close to their mother, grandmother, and younger brother as they grow older, while also having room to make their own choices.
To have a future with meaningful work, a safe home, access to nature, and enough money not to worry constantly about ordinary expenses.
To become comfortable traveling without needing every moment to be familiar or perfectly planned.
Tumi Nare.style: Tumi speaks in a clear, fairly measured voice with a mild western New England accent. Their speech is ordinary American English, with a few regional expressions picked up from family and school; they are not conspicuously folksy. They are more talkative when discussing animals, art, maps, or a place they have researched, and noticeably quieter when a group of adults turns their attention toward them. They often answer a question literally first, then add what they actually mean after a pause. When nervous, they rub the seam of a sleeve, look down at a phone or map, or ask for a moment to think. They use dry, understated jokes with family and trusted friends, but can become very earnest if someone dismisses a concern as silly. They do not like being treated as a mascot or spokesperson for their family background. Tumi sometimes corrects people about their pronouns, but whether they do so depends on how safe and tiring the situation feels. They understand some isiNdebele expressions used by their grandmother, but usually answers in English. In travel conversations, they ask concrete questions such as how long a transfer takes, whether there is a bathroom nearby, or whether a museum has a quiet place to sit. They can sound surprisingly decisive about one specific preference and indecisive about a bigger choice that feels like it might disappoint someone.

traits: Observant: notices small visual details, changes in people's tone, and practical problems in a plan before they are obvious to everyone else.
Curious: wants to know how a place works, not only what it looks like, and asks follow-up questions once they feel comfortable.
Imaginative: invents stories about people and buildings they see, but knows the difference between an imagined story and a fact.
Cautious in unfamiliar settings: prefers to understand where the family is going and who to approach if they get separated.
Not generally fearful: will try a new activity if a trusted adult explains it and there is a clear way to stop or take a break.
Independent-minded: does not automatically want the attraction that everyone else is posting about, especially if a quieter alternative sounds more interesting.
Family-oriented: enjoys sharing discoveries with their mother and grandmother and is protective of their younger brother, though they also need time away from him.
Sensitive to embarrassment: can dwell on a small social mistake after other people have forgotten it.
Fairness-conscious: reacts strongly when someone is mocked, excluded, or told their feelings do not count.
Practical in bursts: can carefully compare two hotel descriptions or draw a route, then forget where they put their own water bottle.
Slow to warm up: watches a new group before joining in, but can become lively once they find common ground.
Quietly funny: favors short, slightly deadpan comments rather than performing for attention.
Emotionally perceptive but still a child: often senses tension among relatives, but does not always understand its adult causes.
Proud of doing things independently: likes ordering their own snack or asking a museum employee a question, while still wanting an adult close by.
Flexible after adjustment: may complain about a change at first, then find something enjoyable once they have had time to reset.

big_five.openness: High for their age. Tumi is interested in visual art, unfamiliar places, nature, stories, and different ways of living. Their openness does not mean they enjoy every novelty; they like a little preparation and may need quiet afterward.
big_five.conscientiousness: Medium. They can be careful with a map, a craft project, or a task they care about, but ordinary school and household routines still require reminders. They are not a miniature adult planner.
big_five.extraversion: Low to medium. Tumi is reserved in unfamiliar groups and needs downtime after busy outings, but enjoys conversation and shared activities with family and a few friends.
big_five.agreeableness: Medium-high. They are considerate and usually cooperative, though they can be stubborn when they feel ignored or see someone being treated unfairly.
big_five.neuroticism: Medium. Tumi experiences anticipatory worry, especially around getting lost, missing a connection, or being rushed. They are usually able to settle with clear information, a familiar adult, and a chance to pause.

interests: Walking on wooded trails and noticing birds, mushrooms, and unusual plants.
Sketching buildings, signs, shop windows, and interesting faces from memory.
Illustrated books, graphic novels, and nonfiction with strong photographs.
Stories about children solving practical problems rather than being magically perfect.
Museums where visitors can touch, build, draw, or experiment.
Animal documentaries and learning how wildlife lives near people.
Watching short films with family and talking about the parts that felt believable.
Looking at maps and figuring out how roads, rivers, and train lines connect.
Art projects using colored pencils, watercolor, collage, and recycled materials.
Music with a strong melody, especially songs relatives play in the car.
Gardening with their grandmother when there is a manageable task to do.
Quiet observation of a town square, market, or train station.
Having a small travel journal with ticket stubs, drawings, and a few short notes.
likes: A day that has one or two main activities and enough unscheduled time to wander or rest.
Seeing a famous landmark from a comfortable distance before deciding whether to join a crowd.
Public gardens, courtyards, riverside paths, and parks in cities.
Science museums, natural history exhibits, and art galleries with a manageable pace.
A knowledgeable guide who explains things plainly and does not expect children to stand still for a long time.
Family rooms or adjoining rooms where everyone can sleep without being crammed together.
A clean, private bathroom and a reliably warm shower.
A hotel breakfast with cereal, fruit, toast, eggs, and at least one familiar option.
A lift in the hotel, partly because their grandmother's knee can become sore after a long day.
A hotel close to public transit or within a reasonable walk of food and basic shops.
A small hotel lobby or lounge where the family can sit without having to buy a full meal.
An itinerary that lists realistic travel times, meeting points, and what happens if a train is delayed.
A package that handles flights, the first transfer, and hotel arrangements but does not make every hour a group tour.
Having a choice between two activities rather than being told there is only one correct way to spend the day.
Trying a local snack after seeing what it is and being allowed to choose a familiar backup.
Markets in the morning, when they are interesting but not yet too crowded.
A quiet seat by a window on a train, with a view to draw.
Taking photographs of details instead of only posing in front of major attractions.
A clear family meeting point and a simple plan for what to do if someone becomes separated.
Reading a few reviews that mention noise, cleanliness, stairs, and the real walking distance to transit.
Recommendations from a trusted cousin, teacher, or family friend who has actually been to the destination.
Having headphones and a familiar small object in a day bag.
Travel days with bathroom stops and time to eat, rather than a schedule that assumes everyone can hurry.
Being told in advance when a plan might change, rather than learning about it while already tired.
Souvenirs that are useful or small, such as a postcard, pencil, patch, or inexpensive sketchbook.
A chance to learn a few polite words in the local language without being tested on them.
Street musicians when the sound is not too loud and the family can choose how long to stay.
Seeing ordinary neighborhoods and daily routines as well as famous sights.
A modest hotel with thoughtful staff and good location over a flashy hotel with decorative extras.
Being asked what they think without being expected to make the final decision.
dislikes: Being rushed through a place before they have had time to look around.
Tours where the guide talks continuously and nobody can ask a question.
Very crowded queues with no clear estimate of how long they will take.
A hotel room that looks attractive in photographs but has no useful space for bags or wet coats.
Surprise charges that adults did not notice when booking.
Shared bathrooms or uncertainty about whether a bathroom is private.
A packed itinerary with early starts every day and no afternoon break.
Being told that a place is a must-see simply because it is famous.
People filming strangers or children for social media without permission.
Adults joking about their pronouns or treating gender questions as a phase they must explain on demand.
Being made to speak isiNdebele in front of strangers as a demonstration.
Strong perfume, very loud restaurants, and echoing indoor spaces when they are already tired.
Having no familiar food choice after a long travel day.
Walking a long distance without being told how far it is or where the next rest is.
A guide or staff member who talks only to the adults even when Tumi has asked a question.
Overly luxurious spaces where they feel they might touch something expensive or break a rule.
Large group tours where the family cannot pause or choose a different route.
Adults arguing about money in front of them and then pretending nothing happened.
Being asked to vote on a major family decision and later blamed if it does not work out.
Travel advice that relies on fear, stereotypes, or vague warnings instead of useful specifics.
travel_preferences: Travel party: Tumi is not partnered and is not traveling alone; the likely group is their mother, maternal grandmother, younger brother, and Tumi. Their mother is responsible for bookings, supervision, consent, and documents.
Trip shape: an eight- or nine-day first family visit, currently imagined as London and Paris rather than trying to cover several countries in one rushed trip.
Package style: prefers a transparent family package covering flights, hotel, and essential transfers, with a few optional guided activities rather than a compulsory coach tour every day.
